## The founder-emulation items

1. **Who (practitioner `agent`).** YC-C names hotel groups with "call centers and central reservation departments";
   YC-L's video features front-desk staff at a Munich hotel. *My choice:* the reservation agent, central office or
   front desk, who sees the missed-call list. Segment: hotel groups in Germany with a central office or call center.
2. **When (circumstance, occasion, window).** YC-L's "After hours. During peak hours. On holidays." *My choice:* the
   occasion "reservation shift", window the last 7 days (calls come in on every shift; spec 120's "every shift" -> 7
   DAYS), Frequency 5 to 7 days out of 7.
3. **Who pays (decision-maker `director`, Buyer and payer, Purchase friction).** TERMS addresses the hotel group;
   YC-L asks to "book a 10-minute call if you lead a hotel group". *My choice:* the revenue or reservations director
   decides, the hotel's owner has to agree. Purchase friction tests "A data protection review of guest calls" (German
   hotels handle guests' card and personal data on the call); my choice, no source names it.
4. **Mechanism.** YC-C: missed calls forwarded to Codyco, the AI answers, bookings appear in the PMS. Compatibility
   tests call forwarding (the mechanism needs it); Adoption friction tests letting the AI answer in the hotel's voice.
5. **Cost, price, ability.** As in the table. Reading `budget` by the engine (a percent of calls against euros).
6. **Commitment.** TERMS and YC-L: the paid, money-back pilot at one location. The step carries its number ("pay
   €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel"), the gap-8 check.

No first-person account by a German reservation agent or revenue director was found in public (no HN thread; the
site's quotes are curated testimonials). **Every person is the author's invention**, no real person's name is used,
and each is built on the public facts named here.

Revenue directors (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3): Stefanie Wagner (6%), Andreas Keller (4%, below the founder's 5%),
Roberto Bianchi (8%), Ingrid Lindholm (2%, a call center covers after hours), Karim Benali (does not know his rate;
YC-L's "Free AI Strategy Workshop" and SITE's free test number as his ask), Petra Vogel (5%), Hannes Moser (nothing,
would not pay), Joanna Wiśniewska (10% at resort hotels in high season). The value boxes are percents of the calls, in
the founder's unit and period; the price picks are two codes, the pilot's rung and the licence's rung, each placed
against the founder's €3,000 and €1,000.

## Status today

Same idea (SITE, 2026-10-22): "Turn missed hotel calls into paid bookings.", widened to payments, invoices and
handovers; "Running at 15+ hotel groups" (the launch said 7); "€10k+ bookings written directly into the PMS". **No
public price today** (SITE and /faq show none); the €3,000 pilot terms remain the only priced source.

## Open (what could not be sourced, and the workarounds)

- **The licence amount** was never public. €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month is the operator's reading of the pilot's
  monthly rate (above). Treat the plan step's reading as a reading of that derivation.
- **Dollars or euros.** YC-L says "$5,000", YC-C "€5,000" for the same hotel; the pilot fee is in euros and the company
  is in Munich, so the entry is in euros. The market is DE, and the golden corpus's rule U (US only) is a note.
- **The "> 8 hotels" / "10 hotels" roll-out threshold** in TERMS and YC-L disagree; the entry does not use it.
- **Job titles.** Neither the agent nor the director is named in public; both are my choices (items 1 and 3).
- **The 5% is the founders' claim** for "the best" offices; no independent figure was sought.
- **UPFRONT_THEN has no "credited" or "money-back" flag**; the fee is a plain up-front amount (header).

screens.why1: Choosing which fit condition to test comes right after I checked the rows Keel reviewed, so it is obvious why I am asked here.
screens.why2: Call forwarding and OPERA Cloud, Sihot or Apaleo as the PMS are everyday words in a German reservations office, and both rows read plainly on first sight.
screens.why3: I know which of my hotel groups have phone systems that forward and which PMS they run, so I can pick from what I actually see.
screens.why4: The two rows are distinct, both are mine, and the one my mechanism hangs on (forwarding missed calls to us) is there to pick.
screens.why5: I wrote could forward unanswered calls, meaning the phone system can do it; were allowed to have them forwarded leans toward someone's permission, close to my meaning but drifted a little toward policy rather than setup.
screens.why7: The picked row is a permission tested against the bar on only with help or approval or no, it is the step the idea depends on most, it is not settled for the whole segment so it can hold or fail, and the PMS row stays as a belief rather than asked.
screens.instead: Which one do you want to test? - Could have unanswered calls forwarded to another number (set up by IT or the phone provider) - Ran OPERA Cloud, Sihot or Apaleo as their PMS

screens.why1: Right after I've said how it fits into what the desk already does, asking what it does better than today's call-backs is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: Short and plain, and 'reservation agents' and 'today's way' are exactly how I talk about the central office and the front desk.
screens.why3: I know what Codyco gives a hotel group that a busy desk or call center doesn't, the 5% of calls that ring out turned into bookings, so I can answer from my own numbers.
screens.why4: It's a box to type in with the single 'I'm not sure' escape chip, which is the right escape for a founder who can't name a benefit.
screens.why5: My two benefits, missed calls turned into bookings and callers answered when the desk is busy, stand as I typed them, one a line.
screens.why7: The screen asks for 1 to 4 benefits of at most 9 words, one a line, framed against today's way, with 'I'm not sure' as the founder's escape, as the card's benefit_list requires.

screens.why1: Right after I typed what it does better, Keel reads my benefits back so I can check them before they become the belief, which is where this belongs.
screens.why2: "Missed calls", "bookings" and "the desk is busy" are how my reservation agents and I talk every shift, so the rows read on first pass.
screens.why3: An agent who just watched a booking call ring out knows whether it would have been answered and booked, so the belief sits on a moment they lived.
screens.why4: The two rows overlap: a caller answered when the desk is busy is mostly how a missed call becomes a booking, so they are close to one gain said twice.
screens.why5: My gain is calls caught after hours, at peak and on holidays, but "when the desk is busy" keeps only the peak and drops the night and holiday calls my launch led with.
screens.why7: The hard case is the right moment (the call that rang out) and the bar fits the four-point scale, but the two rows are near one gain, and "the last time a call rang out would have given them missed calls turned into bookings" mixes one moment with a plural.
screens.instead: Rows: "That missed call answered and booked, any hour" · "The booking written straight into our PMS" -- belief: For most, with it, the last booking call of theirs that rang out would have been answered and booked, straight into their PMS.

screens.why1: Right after what it does better, asking what effort it takes my reservation agents to start is the obvious next question about the solution.
screens.why2: Setup, extra steps, learning: plain words, and the hint's four rows of nine words is clear on first read.
screens.why3: I know exactly what my agents would have to do: let the missed calls go to the AI and pick up whatever it hands back to the desk.
screens.why4: It is a box to type in with *I'm not sure* as the only chip, which is the escape the card allows on my side.
screens.why5: My two rows sit on the screen as I typed them, in *their* voice, unchanged.
screens.why7: Both rows are single efforts in base form and the second is a real new habit, but *start using it* pulls toward setup, which our team and the group's phone system do, and *Hand their missed booking calls to the AI* edges toward a forwarding decision the office or director makes rather than an effort the agent takes alone.
screens.instead: What will your reservation agents have to do differently on a shift once it is running? (e.g. let missed calls go to the AI; take every call it hands back to the desk)

screens.why1: Right after I said what agents will have to do, Keel shows that list back to me to check before I pick the one to test, which is exactly where it belongs.
screens.why2: 'Missed booking calls', 'the desk' and 'hands to the desk' are how we talk in a reservations office; only the doubled 'What they'll have to do' title and intro reads a little clumsy.
screens.why3: Both rows are things my reservation agents would actually feel on a shift: their missed calls going to the AI and the calls it passes back landing on them.
screens.why4: Two distinct efforts, in our words and within the 9-word limit, with nothing missing that I meant to put there.
screens.why5: These are my rows as I saved them, and they still mean what I meant: the agent lets the AI take the missed calls and takes back the ones it hands over.
screens.why7: 'Take every call the AI hands to the desk' is the agent's own new habit, just what the card wants, but 'Hand their missed booking calls to the AI' is really a routing decision the director makes and a forwarding setup that Compatibility already tests, so one row bends the 'a step they take themselves' rule.
screens.instead: Keep 'Take every call the AI hands to the desk' and replace the first row with 'Check the bookings the AI writes into the PMS', which is an effort the agent takes themselves on every shift.

screens.why1: Right after I checked my adoption-friction rows, picking the one effort most likely to stop my agents is the obvious next step before the test is built.
screens.why2: Missed booking calls, the AI, the desk: these are exactly the words my reservation agents and I use every shift, readable on first pass.
screens.why3: An agent who sees the missed-call list knows whether they would let those calls go to an AI and whether they would pick up the hand-offs, so both rows are answerable from their own shift.
screens.why4: The two rows are distinct efforts in my own wording, one letting go of the missed calls and one taking the AI's hand-offs, with nothing nonsensical or doubled.
screens.why5: Both rows are my saved rows word for word and the belief repeats my picked row unchanged, so the screen still means what I typed.
screens.why7: The second row is a clean new habit the agent takes on, but my picked row 'hand their missed booking calls to the AI' reads more as a willingness to give up the calls than an effort of use, and in practice the routing is set by the director or the phone setup (Compatibility's ground), so the measure bends a little even though the belief can still be supported or refuted.
screens.instead: Which effort is most likely to stop them? -- Take every call the AI hands to the desk · Check the bookings the AI wrote into the PMS on their shift

screens.why1: Just before the study goes out is the right moment to decide whether people get a follow-up line, and offering a pilot is exactly what I do with hotel groups.
screens.why2: 'Pilot' is my own word from the Zero Risk Pilot, and the hint spells out what the respondent will see and where I find the yeses.
screens.why3: Whether I want to collect leads for a pilot is my own decision, and I know the answer at once.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it, the two options are distinct, and neither needs an escape.
screens.why5: My pilot is a paid €3,000 money-back pilot at one hotel that a director signs off on, while the line shown here is a generic 'try this for real, leave your email' put to reservation agents, so the offer drifts a little from what I actually sell.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? Respondents who say yes see: "Would your hotel try this at one location? Leave your email and we'll pass it to whoever runs reservations." (Yes, ask them / No pilot)

screens.why1: A save step right before the study goes out, after the pilot offer, is exactly where I'd expect to lock in my answers.
screens.why2: "Save your answers" is plain, but the option "lock and record the face Keel preselects" uses "face" in a way no hotel founder would, and I'd have to read it twice to see it means the interviewer's look.
screens.why3: It asks me only to confirm my own study, which I know fully.
screens.why4: Taking Keel's preselected interviewer face works as a default, but the screen gives no clear way to change it or to save without a face, so the choice feels thin.
screens.why5: Saving changes nothing I typed: the reservation agent, the missed calls and the €3,000 pilot all stand as I wrote them.
screens.instead: Save your answers -- keep the interviewer Keel picked for your study, or choose another face?

screens.why1: Choosing how strangers will take the study is the natural last step before the link goes out, right after saving my answers.
screens.why2: The options are clear, but the question 'New link' is a bare label rather than a question, so I have to read the options to know what is being asked.
screens.why3: I know my reservation agents and directors, and whether they would rather tap on a phone between calls or talk to a video face, so I can answer from what I know.
screens.why4: Read and tap, AI interviewer and let them choose cover the real choices, are distinct, and each says plainly what the respondent does.
screens.why5: Nothing of my idea is restated here, so nothing of what I typed is changed.
screens.instead: How should reservation agents take the study when they open the link? Read and tap / AI interviewer on video / Let them choose

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits under the title with '3 beliefs: 3 holding', each card carries its count against the bar, and 'the verdict is the worst of all its cards' ties them together, so I can see the 5 of 7 on Relative advantage is what decides it.
screens.why_b2: Each card's line says what was counted ('said yes, easily or with some steps', 'would do it'), over how many (of 7) and where the bar sits (5 of 7), so I read all three at once.
screens.why_b3: The dimensions are mine, but the statement stutters ('the hotel the hotel forwards', 'gets back the confirmed booking in the PMS' twice over), and the Relative advantage line ('the last time a reservation call of theirs rang out would have given them missed calls turned into bookings') is a mangled version of what I'd say, so it is recognisable but not in my words.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what to do with a solution that holds, such as moving to the €3,000 pilot ask, or what to do with the 3 who would only hand calls over on a condition; the only text below the cards explains the method.
screens.why_b5: '3 holding' over only 7 agents is never called a small sample, and Relative advantage sitting exactly at the bar (5 of 7) still rolls up to an unqualified 'Holding up'; only the card's small 'at the bar' hints at how thin it is.
screens.instead: Holding up on 7 reservation agents, a small sample: Relative advantage only just clears (5 of 7, the bar), and 3 of the 6 would hand calls over only on a condition, so find out what those conditions are before you put the €3,000 pilot in front of a director.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 6 of 7 said yes against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answers over the 7 who answered (5, 1, 1, 0), and the strip's marker at 5 with 6 cells for sits plainly past it.
screens.why_b3: I recognise it, but I wrote that agents could forward unanswered calls, not that they 'were allowed to'; the bar line 'You said were allowed to...' is clipped, and 'your last booking call' isn't my 'shift with a missed call'.
screens.why_b4: It tells me concretely that call forwarding is not the blocker and points me to Adoption friction as the thing to work on.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible and 'a lean, not a call' is said, but the So line then states flatly that forwarding 'is not what will stop them' and Adoption friction 'is', firmer than 7 people carry, and it passes over Aylin's old phone system the owner won't replace.
screens.instead: Most reservation agents could have their unanswered calls forwarded: 6 of 7 said yes, past your bar of 5, a lean from a small group; the one no was an old phone system the owner won't replace, so ask about the phone system on the first call, and look at Adoption friction next.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 5 of 7 said better against a bar of 5 of 7, and it says at the bar, so I know it held by the narrowest margin and why.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts 7 people as Better 5 (all a lot), Same 1 and Worse 1, and the strip puts the marker at 5 against the bar of 5 of 7, all readable at first look even if Better 5 5 a lot stutters.
screens.why_b3: Both my benefits are in the belief, but the line is clumsy (the time a call rang out would have given them missed calls turned into bookings), and the bar line quotes only my first benefit, so it reads as mine reworded rather than mine as I checked it.
screens.why_b4: The So line only hands off to Adoption friction; it never says that Chiara's group already covers after hours with a call center and Tobias won't put guests on a machine, which is the concrete steer toward groups without after-hours cover.
screens.why_b5: n of 7 stays visible, the screen calls it a lean, not a call, and says at the bar rather than strong; only the count line's last booking call drifts slightly from the rang-out moment that was actually asked.
screens.instead: Held at the bar, 5 of 7, all a lot: the two against already have after-hours cover or won't hand guests to a machine, so lead with groups whose calls go unanswered after six and test that next.

screens.why_b1: The status word Holding up sits right beside 6 of 7 would do it against a bar of 5 of 7, with the 3 on a condition named, so I know the belief held and by what count.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts each of the 7 answers by option, for or against, and the strip shows 6 for and 1 against with the marker at 5 of 7, so what is counted, over how many and where the bar sits are plain at once.
screens.why_b3: Adoption friction and 'Most would hand their missed booking calls to the AI' are the step I picked, in my words, and the question asked my agents the same thing.
screens.why_b4: The So line only repeats the split and points below for what would make it worth it, though the condition, that guests still reach a person, is already on the screen and calls for a concrete move: promise and show the handover to the desk.
screens.why_b5: n of 7 stays visible, the small group is called a lean rather than a call, and half the support being conditional is stated in the verdict line, so nothing overreaches.
screens.instead: Holding up, but half of the six yeses hang on one thing: guests can still reach a person, so lead the pilot pitch with the AI handing every call it can't close straight to the desk.

screens.why_b1: Each box opens on 'Holding up' with its number beside it ('Compatibility held, 6 of 7', 'Relative advantage held, 5 of 7', at the bar), so the verdict and the deciding count are tied together.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility is close to my 'could forward unanswered calls to another number' but now says 'were allowed to', and the Relative advantage line is a clumsy splice ('the last time a reservation call of theirs rang out would have given them missed calls turned into bookings') that I recognise but would never have written.
screens.why_b4: The screen shows the dissenting quotes but never says what they mean for the idea: nothing about checking phone systems before a pilot, or the hotels where a call center already covers nights, and nothing about the 5 of 7 sitting exactly on the bar.
screens.why_b5: The n stays visible on both lines, Murat's absence is named, the 5 of 7 is marked 'at the bar' and not called strong, and nothing is claimed beyond the 1 and 2 people quoted.
screens.why_b6: The quotes add what I did not type: an old phone system that only IT can change and an owner who won't pay to replace it, a group whose call center already covers after six and whose real pain is group emails with no rates, and guests who ring wanting a person who knows the house.

screens.why1: As the first screen it is plainly a screener checking I am the right person, which is obvious and expected.
screens.why2: I understand it, but I would say Zentrale Reservierung or our reservations office; call center and central reservations office as alternatives make me pause on whether both are needed.
screens.why3: I know exactly where I work and that we run a central reservations office in Munich.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it cleanly for a gate, and no escape is right here.
screens.why5: It names the segment in plain trade words and nothing of the product leaks.
screens.why6: It says well enough, but the 'central reservations office or call center' pair is a slight mouthful for one hearing.
screens.instead: Do you work at a hotel group in Germany with a central reservations office? Yes or No.

screens.why1: A gate on last week's booking calls belongs right after the screener, but asking a reservation agent whether a booking call came in on their shift feels pointless, since that is the whole job.
screens.why2: Booking call and shift are my everyday words; I understand it at once.
screens.why3: I know exactly what came in on my shifts last week, Messe Saturday included.
screens.why4: Yes and No are complete and distinct for this question as asked, and the story chips sit with the story box, not the gate.
screens.why5: The founder's problem is calls that don't get answered, but the screen asks only whether a call came in, so the costly part (the missed or ringing-out call) is dropped and the meaning is wrong.
screens.why6: Short, one question, and 'Yes or no' is easy to hold when heard.
screens.why7: The gate asks the circumstance every agent shares (calls come in on every shift), so every one of us says Yes, No has nobody, and the founder's share can never be refuted; this is the card's bad example.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did a booking call to your office ring out without anyone answering? Yes or no.

screens.why1: After asking whether a booking call came in on my shift, it's obvious why the idea is shown now, before the part about it.
screens.why2: PMS, OPERA Cloud, Sihot and Apaleo are my everyday words, but in a central reservations office 'the desk' is unclear: does it mean us agents, or a hotel's front desk?
screens.why3: Missed calls at peak, the booking going into the PMS, and taking card payment on the phone are exactly what I handle on a trade-fair Saturday.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: It reads as the founder's idea shown on purpose, in my trade's words, with nothing leaking beyond the card itself.
screens.why6: Heard once it's long, at six sentences with a list of three systems, and the belief repeats 'the confirmed booking in your PMS' instead of pointing back to the how.
screens.instead: Imagine Codyco, an AI reservation agent that answers the calls nobody picks up. When no one picks up, the call goes to it; it answers the guest in your hotel's voice, takes the payment, and books straight into your PMS, such as OPERA Cloud, Sihot or Apaleo. It passes a call to one of us by rules you set. The people building it believe those missed calls would end up as confirmed bookings.

screens.why1: Right after the card about an AI that answers the calls nobody picks up, asking whether our missed calls could even be sent somewhere else is the obvious first thing to check.
screens.why2: Forwarding unanswered calls to another number is everyday talk in a reservations office, and I get it on one hearing.
screens.why3: I know our phones roll over to colleagues at peak, but whether IT could send them to an outside number I would partly be guessing, and that setting has nothing to do with my last call in particular.
screens.why4: The four answers cover it: it's a switch IT flips, it takes some setup, it needs the head of reservations or telephony provider to sign off, or no; I can't tell fits too.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product's name or plan comes through in the question itself; 'another number' stays neutral.
screens.why6: Short stem, four short options read as a list, one escape at the end: easy to hold on the phone.
screens.why7: It is a permission row with the passive stem, the registry's four in order and I can't tell apart; offices differ on whether calls can leave the system, so it can go either way, and it tests the step the idea rests on.
screens.instead: Think of your phone system at work. Could unanswered booking calls have been sent on to an outside number? Yes, easily · Yes, with some steps · Only with help or approval · No · I can't tell

screens.why1: Right after the idea card it is obvious why I'm asked whether this AI would have done better on a call nobody picked up.
screens.why2: I had to read it twice, because 'helped you turn every guest who calls into a booking better' is clumsy, and 'turn every guest into a booking' is a target from a manager's slide, not how I'd say it; I'd say 'take the booking'.
screens.why3: In a central office a call that rings out mostly goes into the queue or abandoned-call stats, so I only partly know when one was missed and what that guest wanted, and I'd half guess.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference, worse and I can't tell cover what I'd say, and 'worse' is a real answer if a bot mangles a trade-fair group booking.
screens.why5: The founder's own job line, 'turn every guest who calls into a booking', reached me word for word and reads like their pitch rather than my work.
screens.why6: The stem runs well past twenty words and the job clause is a mouthful to hold before the four options come, though the list itself says fine.
screens.why7: There are four fixed rungs on one measure, two for and two against, the hard case is the moment the call went unanswered, the job is named, no benefit is shown, and I can't tell is set apart.
screens.instead: Think of the most recent time a booking call rang out with nobody to pick it up. Would Codyco, an AI reservation agent, have helped you get that booking, or not? A lot better · A little better · No difference · Worse · I can't tell

screens.why1: As the last idea question it makes sense to ask what it would take from me to start using the thing just shown, and it is a different question from screen 4, which asked whether calls could be forwarded at all.
screens.why2: Missed booking calls and handing them over are how we talk in the reservations office, so I understand it on first hearing.
screens.why3: Where unanswered calls go is set in our phone system by the team lead and IT, not by me on my shift, so I would partly be guessing whether I would be the one doing the handing over.
screens.why4: The four answers are distinct and complete, and 'only if guests still reach a person' is exactly my real condition on a trade-fair Saturday, with 'I can't tell' fitting as the escape.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks beyond the idea card shown on purpose, and the founder's 'missed booking calls' comes through in words I would use myself.
screens.why6: Spoken it is one short question with four short options I can hold, then the single escape.
screens.why7: The options are on the one measure, in the card's order, with my own condition and the escape, but the 'effort' is less a step I take myself (setup, learning, a new habit) than accepting a routing change that our office's phone setup and lead decide, so the rule that it be my own effort is bent.
screens.instead: To use Codyco, you'd check the bookings the AI took at the start of each shift. Would you do that, or not? Yes · Only if it flags the unclear ones · Probably not · No · I can't tell.
